reason: The sources provide over 15 multi-verified facts detailing the discovery, mass, collision speed, and astrophysical implications of El Gordo.
story: Over seven billion light-years from Earth lies a cosmic colossus so massive that astronomers named it El Gordo, Spanish for 'The Fat One'. Discovered using telescopes in Chile and NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, this titan weighs as much as three quadrillion times the mass of our Sun. But El Gordo is not a single peaceful cluster. It is a catastrophic collision between two separate galaxy subclusters smashing into each other at millions of miles per hour. The violent impact wretches normal matter apart, slowing down superheated X-ray gas while unseen dark matter sails straight through unhindered. This sheer concentration of matter warps spacetime itself into a cosmic magnifying glass, bending the light of background galaxies behind it. Representing the most massive and X-ray bright cluster ever found at such an immense distance, El Gordo pushes the very limits of our cosmic models.
angle: Two galaxy clusters weighing three quadrillion suns are colliding at millions of miles per hour, wrenching normal matter completely away from dark matter.

claims.claim: The galaxy cluster carries the formal astronomical catalog designation ACT-CL J0102-4915.
Astronomers nicknamed the cluster 'El Gordo', which translates from Spanish to 'the Fat One'.
The cluster is located in the southern sky constellation of Phoenix.
Results detailing El Gordo were first announced at the 219th meeting of the American Astronomical Society in Austin, Texas.
The cluster was detected by the Atacama Cosmology Telescope located in northern Chile.
NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory was used to observe and analyze the cluster's hot gas.
The European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope was used to measure galaxy velocities and distance.
El Gordo is an interacting merger composed of two separate galaxy subclusters.
The two subclusters are colliding at speeds of several million kilometers per hour.
El Gordo is the most massive galaxy cluster discovered at its distance or beyond.
The cluster produces the most X-rays of any known galaxy cluster observed at its distance or beyond.
Astronomers estimated the cluster contains as much as three quadrillion (three million billion) times the mass of the Sun.
The cluster formed through an interaction similar to the Bullet Cluster, marking the first time such a system was discovered at such a great distance.
During the merger, normal matter made of hot gas slowed down and was wrenched away from dark matter, which was not slowed.
El Gordo's gigantic mass acts as a gravitational lens that bends and distorts the images of distant background galaxies behind it.
Astrophysicist Jack Hughes of Rutgers University served as an investigator analyzing the cluster.

disputed: Distance estimates vary among sources: S1, S3, and S5 state approximately 7 billion light-years, S6 and S7 cite 7.3 billion light-years, while S2 lists 9.7 billion light-years; the script should attribute the distance as roughly 7 billion light-years.

Total mass estimates range from two million billion times the mass of the Sun (S5) to three million billion / three quadrillion solar masses (S4, S6, S7), with S1 noting an initial estimate slightly below three quadrillion later refined to 2.1 quadrillion solar masses; scripts should state the mass spans two to three quadrillion solar masses.

Cosmological model consistency: S3 reports the cluster is consistent with standard dark matter and Big Bang models, while S1 documents scientific arguments that its high collision speed and huge mass challenge the standard Lambda-CDM model; the script should present this as an ongoing scientific debate.
